column2: Rootstock from a Vitis riparia × V. rupestris cross, bred in France in the 1880s. It is low-vigor and advances ripening, suited to fertile, moist soils, but it tolerates little drought or lime.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. rupestris cross. It is vigorous and drought-tolerant, widely used in dry Mediterranean vineyards.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. rupestris cross, bred in Sicily. It is vigorous and tolerates drought and moderate salinity.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. rupestris cross, bred in Sicily. It is very vigorous and tolerates drought and limestone soils.
Rootstock bred in France from a Vitis solonis × V. riparia cross. It is low-vigor and tolerates wet and somewhat saline soils.
Rootstock from a Vitis riparia × V. rupestris cross. Moderately low in vigor and widely used in cool, deep, well-watered soils; it handles drought and lime poorly.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. riparia cross. Low vigor, lime-tolerant and slow to establish; common in Champagne and Burgundy.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. riparia cross, selected by Kober in Austria. It is vigorous and lime-tolerant.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. riparia cross, selected in Hungary. Moderate vigor and early ripening.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. rupestris cross. Vigorous and drought-tolerant, used in warm regions.
Wood of the black locust tree (Robinia pseudoacacia), sometimes used for white-wine barrels. It is commonly described as giving floral notes with little oak-style spice.
Red grape of Nemea in the Peloponnese, Greece. It makes soft, fruity reds as well as rosés.
White grape of Burgundy, typically high in acidity. It is used for Bourgogne Aligoté and, traditionally, for the Kir cocktail.
French département whose forests (including Tronçais) supply tight-grained sessile oak prized for wine barrels.
Brazilian hardwood (Amburana cearensis) used for casks, especially for cachaça. It gives strong sweet-spice aromas often compared to cinnamon.
The main American barrel oak. Its staves are usually sawn rather than split, and it typically gives stronger vanilla and coconut notes than French oak.
Portuguese white grape that keeps high acidity even in warm climates. It is important in Bucelas and Vinho Verde (as Pedernã).
White grape of Roero in Piedmont, Italy, making aromatic, medium-bodied dry whites.
High-acid white grape originally from the Greek island of Santorini, making mineral, dry whites.
French-American hybrid red grape bred by François Baco from Folle Blanche and a Vitis riparia. It is grown in cool climates such as Ontario and New York.
Thick-skinned, high-acid, tannic red grape of Bairrada, Portugal. It is also used for sparkling wine.
High-acid, low-tannin red grape of Piedmont, Italy (e.g. Barbera d'Asti, Barbera d'Alba).

German/Austrian Prädikat levels for sweet wines from individually selected overripe berries, often affected by noble rot. Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) uses shriveled, raisined berries and is the sweeter of the two.
Oak forest in the Nièvre, France, known for fine-grained sessile oak for barrels.
Vine training in which a permanent arm (cordon) extends in two directions along a wire. Short spurs on the cordon are pruned each winter.
Central European red grape, Austria's leading red in Burgenland and called Kékfrankos in Hungary. It typically makes peppery, dark-fruited, fresh reds.
Combining wines from different grapes, vineyards, vessels or vintages to build balance and a consistent style.
Preventing malolactic fermentation (for example by cold, sulfur dioxide or filtration) so the wine keeps its sharper malic acidity.
Very small cask of about 40 litres. Its high wood-to-liquid ratio speeds wood extraction.
Red grape of Utiel-Requena in Valencia, Spain. It is deeply colored and used for reds and rosés.
Argentina's widely planted red Bonarda, identified as Douce Noir (Corbeau) from Savoie. It is not the same as Italian Bonarda.
German fungus-resistant (PIWI) red grape bred at Freiburg with Cabernet Sauvignon as a parent.
A widely planted French certified clone of Cabernet Sauvignon. It is known for small clusters and concentrated fruit.
Winter pruning that keeps one or two of last year's canes and ties them along the wire to bear the new crop. The Guyot system is an example.
Presence of dissolved CO2, which makes wine sparkling. It comes either from a second fermentation or from injected gas.
Late-ripening, high-acid, high-tannin red grape (Cariñena/Mazuelo in Spain). It is common in southern France, Priorat and Sardinia.
Bronze-skinned muscadine (Vitis rotundifolia) variety grown in the southeastern US for wine and juice.
Red Bordeaux grape that is now rare in France. It survived in Chile, where it was long mistaken for Merlot until identified in 1994.
Widely planted red grape of southern Portugal, also called Periquita.
American pink-red grape of Vitis labrusca heritage. It was historically important for 19th-century Ohio sparkling wine.
French-American hybrid red grape, popular in the eastern US for its disease resistance and deep color.
One of the Burgundian 'Dijon' clones of Chardonnay, selected in France and widely planted in Oregon and elsewhere.
A Burgundian 'Dijon' clone of Chardonnay, used for still and sparkling wine.
Aromatic, Muscat-scented clonal variants of Chardonnay.
The Wente selection, the historic Chardonnay clonal lineage behind much of California's Chardonnay. It is known for small, uneven ('hen and chicken') berries.
White grape most associated with Switzerland (Fendant in Valais). It makes delicate, low-acid dry whites.
Cherry wood, occasionally used for casks. It is commonly described as oxidizing wine faster and adding fruity, lightly sweet notes.
Sweet chestnut wood, historically used for barrels in Italy and France. It is porous and low in aromatic compounds, so it allows oxygen exchange.
Heat-tolerant red grape of southern France, used widely in rosé and light reds. It is a parent of Pinotage.
White grape of southern France, used for Clairette de Die sparkling wine and in Rhône blends.
Letting freshly pressed white juice rest cold so solids settle out before fermentation.
White grape of southwest France, used for Cognac and Armagnac distillation and for fresh whites such as Côtes de Gascogne.
Fermenting at low temperatures (often around 10–16 °C for whites) to keep fresh, fruity aromas.
White grape of Piedmont, used for Gavi.
Main red grape of Valpolicella, Bardolino and Amarone.
Plants grown between vine rows to manage soil erosion, structure, water and vine vigor.
Red wine made normally, then with most alcohol removed (e.g. by vacuum distillation or membranes). It is labeled non-alcoholic at or below 0.5% ABV.
Rosé wine with most alcohol removed after fermentation, typically to 0.5% ABV or less.
Sparkling wine with alcohol removed and carbonation restored, typically to 0.5% ABV or less.
White wine with most alcohol removed after fermentation, typically to 0.5% ABV or less.
Separating grape berries from their stems before crushing or fermentation.
Rosé made by pressing red grapes right away, giving brief skin contact and pale color.
Swiss fungus-resistant red grape bred by Agroscope, with Gamaret as a parent.
Vigorous rootstock selection of Vitis champinii, tolerant of nematodes and drought.
Early-ripening red grape of Piedmont, making soft, fruity reds for early drinking.
Cane-pruning system that keeps two canes, one trained each way along the wire.
Draining fermenting red juice off the skins into another tank, then pouring it back over the cap to extract gently.
White grape of the Dão region, Portugal, used for structured dry whites.
Madeira method of heating wine in tanks (estufas) to speed up aging.
Leaving red wine on its skins after fermentation ends to change tannin texture.
Ancient white grape of Campania, Italy.
Red grape of southwest France (e.g. Marcillac), also called Mansois or Braucol.
Indigenous red grape of Romania and Moldova.
White grape of Campania, Italy, best known for Fiano di Avellino.
Passing wine through a filter medium to remove yeast, bacteria or haze before bottling.
A cask used for the first time after its previous contents (e.g. first-fill ex-bourbon), giving more flavor than refill casks.
Large wooden vat, often over 1,000 L. Its low wood-to-liquid ratio gives little oak flavor.
Traditional-method sparkling wine DOCG from Lombardy, Italy. It is made mainly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Nematode-resistant rootstock with Vitis champinii in its parentage, used in California.
European oak species, more porous and higher in tannin than sessile oak. It is traditionally preferred for spirits such as Cognac.
European oak species with tighter grain and more aromatic compounds, widely preferred for wine barrels.
White grape of Friuli, Italy, formerly called Tocai Friulano (identical to Sauvignonasse).
White grape of Friuli and Slovenia (Rebula), often made in skin-contact amber styles.
Cold-hardy red hybrid grape from the University of Minnesota.
Teinturier (red-fleshed) mutation of Gamay.
Main white grape of Soave, Veneto.
Divided-canopy trellis developed at Geneva, New York, with two hanging curtains of shoots.
Georgian tradition of fermenting and aging wine, often with skins, in large buried clay vessels (qvevri). It is on UNESCO's intangible-heritage list.
Free-standing vine trained without wires into a goblet shape, common in hot, dry regions.
White grape of northwest Spain (Valdeorras, Bierzo).
Red grape of Rioja, used in small amounts for acidity, color and aroma.
Teinturier red grape bred by Henri Bouschet.
White grape of Campania, Italy (e.g. Greco di Tufo).
White-skinned form of Grenache, used in the Rhône, Roussillon and Spain.
Grey-pink-skinned form of Grenache, notable in Roussillon.
White grape of southwest France (Jurançon, Gascony), used for dry and sweet wines.
Nematode-resistant rootstock used in California.
Barrel interior toasted long and hot, giving roasted, smoky, coffee-like flavors.
Trimming the tops and sides of the vine canopy during the growing season.
Sessile oak from Hungary's forests (e.g. Zemplén), used for barrels.
Hungarian white grape, the second main grape of Tokaji.
American hybrid grape of Vitis labrusca origin, with 'foxy' flavor.
American red grape of labrusca type, historically used in the eastern US.
German fungus-resistant (PIWI) white grape bred at Freiburg with Riesling as a parent.
Oak forest in the Sarthe, France, used for barrels.
Red grape of Hungary and the Balkans, traditionally used in Bikavér.
Basque drink of red wine mixed with cola, roughly half and half.
German white cross of Trollinger (Schiava) and Riesling.
Barrel staves dried quickly in kilns rather than seasoned outdoors.
Cold-hardy white hybrid grape from the University of Minnesota, with apricot-citrus aromas.
Red grape of Alto Adige, Italy.
Family of red grapes and frizzante wines from Emilia-Romagna.
Grapes picked later than normal for higher sugar, used to make sweeter wines.
Removing leaves around the grape clusters to improve air flow and sun exposure.
Barrel interior toasted briefly, keeping fresh wood character and less roasted flavor.
Oak forests near Limoges, France, with wide-grained, tannic oak traditionally used for Cognac.
Aromatic white grape of Vinho Verde, Portugal.
Divided-canopy trellis shaped like a U or lyre.
White grape of Spain (called Viura in Rioja), one of the classic Cava grapes.
Fortified wine from the Portuguese island of Madeira. It is aged with heat and oxygen, making it very long-lived.
Bronze-skinned muscadine variety grown in the southeastern US.
These American Vitis species are used mainly as parents of phylloxera-resistant rootstocks, not for wine; see the Rootstocks group.
Aromatic Greek white grape revived from near-extinction in the late 20th century.
Cold-hardy red hybrid grape from the University of Minnesota, a grandchild of Pinot Noir.
Fortified wine from western Sicily, made dry to sweet in several aging categories.
White grape of the northern Rhône (Hermitage, Saint-Joseph), often blended with Roussanne.
French-American hybrid red grape suited to cool climates.
White grape of Gaillac and Limoux, used in Blanquette de Limoux.
Indigenous red grape of Bulgaria (Thracian Valley).
Middle toast level for barrels, balancing fresh oak with vanilla and toasty notes.
Toast level between medium and heavy, giving more caramel and spice.
White grape of Muscadet in the western Loire, often aged on its lees (sur lie).
Red grape of northwest Spain (Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra), identical to Portugal's Jaen.
Japanese oak used for whisky casks. It is porous and hard to work, and is associated with sandalwood and incense aromas.
Red grape of Savoie, France.
Red grape widely planted in central Italy (e.g. Montepulciano d'Abruzzo). It is not related to the Tuscan town of Montepulciano.
Lightly sparkling, sweet, low-alcohol wine from Moscato Bianco grapes in Piedmont.
Pink-skinned aromatic Greek grape of Mantinia, Peloponnese.
Wine heated with spices, sugar and often citrus.
German fungus-resistant (PIWI) aromatic white grape with Solaris and Muscat parentage.
Ancient aromatic white Muscat grape, used for wine, table grapes and raisins.
White cross of Riesling and Madeleine Royale, bred in Geisenheim in 1882. It is high-yielding and early-ripening.
Red grape of Etna, Sicily, making pale, perfumed reds.
Sicily's leading red grape.
Barrels used several times that now give little oak flavor but still allow slow oxygen exchange.
Oak forests of the Nièvre, France, known for fine-grained oak.
A barrel used for the first time, giving the most oak flavor and tannin.
White American grape of labrusca type, used for sweet wine and juice.
Spanish legal aging term (Ley 24/2003) for wine aged at least 18 months in total.
Native American red grape (Vitis aestivalis lineage), Missouri's state grape.
Red grape of Fronton, southwest France.
Drying barrel staves outdoors so rain and sun leach harsh tannins before coopering.
Oak native to the Pacific Northwest, sometimes used for wine barrels.
White Catalan grape, one of the three traditional Cava grapes.
Historic red grape of Chile, brought by Spanish settlers (Listán Prieto in Spain).
Share of a wine aged in brand-new barrels, which controls how much oak flavor it gets.
Overhead trellis system, traditional in parts of Italy and northwest Spain.
Teinturier red grape bred by Louis Bouschet from Aramon and Teinturier du Cher. It is a parent of Alicante Bouschet.
White grape of Jurançon with small, thick-skinned berries, used for sweet and dry wines.
Late-ripening red Bordeaux grape, used in small amounts for color and tannin.
White grape of the Valais, Switzerland.
Grape of the Languedoc, best known for high-acid Picpoul de Pinet whites.
White mutation of Pinot Noir, grown in Alsace, Italy (Pinot Bianco) and Germany (Weissburgunder).
Pink-grey-skinned color mutation of Pinot Noir.
Red grape related to Pinot Noir, with downy leaves. It is one of Champagne's three main grapes.
Meunier is a periclinal chimera: its outer cell layer carries a mutation that the inner tissue of Pinot Noir lacks.
Widely planted Burgundian 'Dijon' clone of Pinot Noir.
Burgundian 'Dijon' clone of Pinot Noir with small clusters.
Burgundian 'Dijon' clone of Pinot Noir, known for deep color and dark fruit.
Pinot Noir selection from Burgundy distributed by UC Davis, important in Oregon and California.
Swiss-origin Pinot Noir selection distributed by UC Davis.
South African red cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsault (then called Hermitage), created in 1925.
Croatian red grape of the Dalmatian coast, an offspring of Tribidrag (Zinfandel).
Fortified wine from the Douro Valley, Portugal. Ruby styles keep fresh fruit, Tawny styles are aged oxidatively in wood, and Vintage Port comes from a single declared year.
Traditional Douro cask, used for Port and later often for whisky finishing.
Adding spirit after fermentation has finished, leaving a dry base that may be sweetened later. Sherry is the classic example.
Pale-skinned red grape of the Jura (also called Ploussard).
Red grape of León, Spain.
Pale dry rosé from Provence, France's largest rosé-producing region.
Large cask used for wine, rum and whisky.
Small cask that speeds up spirit maturation.

column1: Rain & sun leaching of harsh tannins
column2: The effect of outdoor seasoning on staves: weather washes out bitter tannins and starts breaking down wood compounds.
Very vigorous Vitis champinii rootstock, tolerant of nematodes, drought and salinity.
Sweet wine of the Veneto made from dried grapes (appassimento), e.g. Recioto della Valpolicella.
A cask reused after its first fill, giving less flavor each time.
German fungus-resistant (PIWI) red grape bred at Geilweilerhof.
A used cask that has been scraped and re-toasted or re-charred to restore some of its flavor.
Pure Vitis riparia rootstock selection. Low vigor and early ripening, suited to fertile soils.
High-acid white grape of Georgia, widely planted across the former USSR.
Spanish rosé tradition of Navarra, typically made from Garnacha.
Italian term for rosé.
Aromatic white grape of the northern Rhône, often blended with Marsanne.
Californian teinturier hybrid grape, used for color and juice.
Vitis rupestris rootstock, deep-rooting and vigorous.
Rootstock from a Vitis berlandieri × V. riparia cross (Selection Oppenheim 4).
Very tannic red grape of Montefalco, Umbria.
Local name for the Sangiovese biotype used for Brunello di Montalcino.
Spanish punch of wine, fruit, sweetener and often brandy.
Teinturier red grape of Georgia, deeply colored.
Pink-skinned mutation of Sauvignon Blanc.
Jura white grape used for Vin Jaune. It is the same variety as Traminer.
Red grape of Alto Adige (Vernatsch, Trollinger), making light reds.
Rootstock from a Vitis riparia × V. rupestris cross with some nematode tolerance.
Divided vertical trellis with upper shoots trained up and lower shoots trained down.
Bronze muscadine (Vitis rotundifolia) variety, the original muscadine named in North Carolina.
Cross-reference: barrel char levels (#1–#4) are covered in the Spirits Academy.
German and Austrian term for sparkling wine.
French-American hybrid white grape grown in England, New York and Canada.
Fortified wines from the Jerez area of Andalusia, aged in soleras. Fino and Manzanilla age under flor, Oloroso ages oxidatively, Amontillado does both, and PX is sweet.
Training the season's new shoots into place on the trellis.
Removing excess or poorly placed shoots early in the season.
White grape grown mainly in Franken and Rheinhessen, Germany, and in Alsace (Sylvaner).
Cane-pruning system that keeps one cane plus a renewal spur.
Amber or orange wines from Goriška Brda, Slovenia, made from white grapes macerated on their skins.
Divided vertical trellis with upward and downward shoots, devised by Richard Smart and John Dyson.
Early-ripening German fungus-resistant (PIWI) white grape, suited to very cool climates.
German fungus-resistant (PIWI) white grape bred at Freiburg.
Training with little shoot positioning, letting the canopy hang freely.
Wine mixed with sparkling water.
Winter pruning of last year's canes down to short spurs on a permanent cordon.
Austrian red grape related to the Pinot family, a parent of Zweigelt.
Very tannic red grape of Madiran, France, and Uruguay's signature grape.
Rhône appellation that makes only rosé.
Red grape of Trentino, Italy.
Barrel ends (heads) toasted like the staves, adding more toast flavor.
Hungarian sweet wine made by adding botrytized (aszú) berries to base wine or must.
Aromatic white grape and Argentina's signature white.
Widely planted Port and Douro red grape.
Hybrid white grape from Gewürztraminer parentage, bred in the US.
Sparkling method with second fermentation in bottle, after which the wine is transferred to a tank, filtered and rebottled.
Family of high-yield white Italian grapes (Ugni Blanc in France).
Famous oak forest in the Allier, France, planted under Colbert, with tight-grained oak.
Red grape of the Jura, also grown in Portugal as Bastardo.
Barrel heads left untoasted, keeping more raw-wood character.
White grape of Rueda, Spain.
White grape of the Marche, Italy.
White grape of Sardinia, Liguria and Provence (Rolle).
French-American hybrid white grape, widely used for Canadian icewine.
Tuscan dessert wine made from dried grapes and aged in small casks (caratelli).
North American vine species native to Texas, valued as a rootstock parent for lime tolerance.
North American vine species, cold-hardy and phylloxera-resistant, used as a rootstock parent.
North American vine species, deep-rooting, used as a rootstock parent.
Oak forests of the Vosges mountains, France, used for barrels.
Central European white grape (Graševina, Olaszrizling), unrelated to Riesling.
Off-dry pink wine from Zinfandel, popularized in California in the 1970s–80s.
Pressing whole clusters without crushing, giving cleaner, lower-phenolic juice.
Wine-based drink mixed with fruit juice, sugar and carbonation.
Catalan white grape, one of the three traditional Cava grapes.
High-acid, tannic red grape of Naoussa, northern Greece.
Austria's most planted red grape, a cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent.
